title: P0 streaming session serialization bottleneck — retrospective
content:
Summary:

On 2026-04-18 we experienced a high-severity degradation of the hosted streaming API where streaming client sessions stalled and a subset of requests incurred 5–30s tail latency, with correlated increases in transient 5xx errors from the streaming frontends. The incident lasted ~72 minutes from detection to full mitigation and caused degraded UX for ~18% of live streaming sessions (estimated).

High level cause (short):
Background serialization of streaming session state (session-checkpoint writes) became CPU- and IO-bound under a traffic pattern with many short-lived sessions and burst reconnects. The serialization worker pool blocked due to a blocking compression call combined with synchronous writes to the session-store, which in turn starved the per-connection IO threads and caused request handling to queue up -> increased p99 latency and origin 5xx when queue limits were hit.

Impact:
- Duration: 2026-04-18 15:07 UTC -> 16:19 UTC (partial mitigation at 15:52 UTC; full mitigation 16:19 UTC).
- Affected: ~18% streaming sessions (estimated from sampled logs), primarily clients using reconnects and session-pinning.
- Symptoms: streaming stalls (no tokens for >5s), connection resets with 502 from edge, elevated frontend CPU on streaming host pool, increased queue depth on streaming request dispatcher.
- Customer visible: chat UIs freezing, partial message duplication on reconnect, higher error rates for streaming endpoints.

Detection:
- First alert (SRE latency-detector) fired at 15:08 UTC: p95 streaming response time exceeded threshold.
- Pager duty triggered; on-call (Maya) paged at 15:09 UTC.
- Slack #sre-streaming thread created and linked in artifacts.

Initial triage notes (on-call):
- Checked region metrics: streaming-host CPU spiked on a subset of instances.
- Observed long blocking syscalls in thread dumps for streaming-worker process (blocked on writes and compress calls).
- Session-store (Redis) latency was elevated but within normal percentile — pointed away from pure Redis outage.
- Correlated increase in small session create/delete events (many short sessions).

Immediate mitigations applied (timeline):
- 15:20 UTC: Throttled incoming new streaming session creation at edge (rate limit) to reduce churn. Immediate reduction in newly created sessions but existing stalls persisted. (Mitigation owner: Maya)
- 15:32 UTC: Disabled background compression for session-checkpoints via runtime flag (quick rollback) to reduce CPU blocking on serialization. Observed some reduction in CPU but queueing remained. (Owner: Liam)
- 15:52 UTC: Flipped session-persistence mode to best-effort (no synchronous session-store writes on every checkpoint) via config flip; this removed blocking writes from the critical path and p99 latency dropped noticeably. (Owner: Ravi)
- 16:19 UTC: Rebalanced streaming host pool and restarted a subset of healthy hosts to clear stuck threads and reclaimed capacity. Full traffic restored. (Owner: Alexei)

Root cause analysis (detailed):
- Feature background: we persist streaming "checkpoints" that include small KV-cache deltas + connection metadata to the session-store so clients can reconnect seamlessly. Checkpoint serialization includes an LZ4 compression and a synchronous write to the session-store (for durability). To avoid data loss we used a small worker pool that handled serialization and writes.
- Under normal workload the worker pool handles throughput. During the observed traffic burst there was a sudden increase in short-lived sessions which increased checkpoint frequency per-second by ~6x on affected hosts.
- The compression step for many small payloads is inefficient: compressed payload sizes were close to the originals and CPU overhead per checkpoint dominated. Compression was not CPU-vectorized on the host binary path we were running (we had a fallback non-optimized path for small payloads following a recent change in the runtime's compression layering).
- Worker pool size was conservative to control NFS/network write concurrency. Because writes were synchronous and each worker spent >50ms per checkpoint on compression+write under burst, the pool hit saturation. Backpressure propagated: checkpoint workers hold locks used by the per-connection IO loop for session state; when workers stalled, IO threads were blocked waiting for locks -> per-connection event loop latency increased and requests queued at the dispatcher. When dispatcher queue exceeded configured backpressure thresholds, frontends returned 5xx.
- Contributing factors:
  - Recent change (serving-runtime PR #1847) swapped to the generic compression wrapper which disabled the optimized path for small payloads (regression).
  - Session persistence writes remain synchronous to guarantee reconnect correctness; no async fallback was in place.
  - No adaptive autoscaling for worker pool (fixed size) and no circuit-breaker when session-store writes exceed latency budget.

Why the existing runbook didn't help immediately:
- Runbook had guidance to "scale worker pool" and "disable persistence" but steps were scattered and expected CLI flags that were not present in the deployed config build (config name mismatch). That caused some time loss while operators found the correct runtime flag.

Logs and evidence pointers (samples):
- Thread dumps: shows threads blocked on Compression::compress() in serving-runtime at ~15:14 UTC (attached in incident artifacts).
- Metrics: checkpoint-per-second spiked from baseline ~120 -> 730 on affected hosts. Worker pool queue length increased beyond 256.
- Traces: distributed traces show long serialization spans in the session-checkpoint span.
- Jira: SRE-4523 (inc triage + follow-ups).

Post-incident actions (short term):
1) Fix and revert regression in compression wrapper (PR open): serving-runtime PR #1847 to restore optimized small-payload path. Owner: Liam. ETA: 2026-04-22.
2) Add a hot-config flag alias in the runtime so runbook steps map to a stable flag name (session.persist.mode and session.persist.sync) and document in runbook. Owner: Maya. ETA: 2026-04-20.
3) Add a circuit-breaker: if checkpoint worker queue > 128 for > 30s, switch to best-effort async persistence automatically. Owner: Ravi. ETA: 2026-05-02.
4) Make compression elective: for payload < 1KB skip compression path. Owner: Alexei. ETA: 2026-04-25.
5) Improve runbook: consolidate steps for "streaming stalls" into a single section with exact flag names + verification queries. Owner: Maya. ETA: 2026-04-21.
6) Post-incident customer comms: CS to prepare a short note for customers that were impacted. Owner: Sofia. ETA: 2026-04-20.

Longer term (system changes):
- Implement per-host adaptive worker pool sizing driven by observed checkpoint-rate.
- Consider moving session persistence writes to an append-only log with eventual compaction to decouple critical path latency.
- Add synthetic traffic test to surface short-session churn and ensure compression path is exercised in canary.

Runbook updates (draft notes):
- New section: "Streaming stalls with high checkpoint rate"
  - Detection: p95 streaming latency > 2s and worker-pool queue > 64 for > 2mins.
  - Immediate steps (ordered):
    1) Check checkpoint-per-second metric by host group (metrics query provided). If > 4x baseline, consider throttling new sessions at edge.
    2) If worker queue > 128, flip session.persist.mode -> best-effort (config alias: session.persist.mode=best-effort).
    3) If CPU on streaming hosts > 80% and p50 compression span > 30ms, disable compression: session.persist.compress=false.
    4) If frontends return >1% 5xx for streaming, drain and restart hosts with blocked threads.
  - Verification: p95 latency returns under 800ms and worker queue drains below 16 within 10 mins.
  - Post-mitigation checklist: capture thread dump, snapshot worker queue metrics, escalate to eng-runtime if compression path is root cause.

On-call notes and questions (unresolved):
- Why did PR #1847 land without test coverage for the small-payload compression path? Need to add unit/integration tests.
- Can we add a telemetry metric specifically for "checkpoint compression time" to make this faster to detect?
- Are there customers relying on strict durability guarantees for session checkpoints? CS to confirm (Sofia).

Communication and follow-up meetings:
- Incident review scheduled: 2026-04-21 16:00 UTC (eng-runtime + SRE + product-hosted-api).
- Engineering bug triage scheduled same day to prioritize regression fix.

Appendix: quick commands and queries (for runbook):
- Check checkpoint rate by host-set: METRICS query: sum(rate(session_checkpoint_count[1m])) by (host_set)
- Check worker queue length: METRICS query: serving_streaming_checkpoint_worker_queue_length{host=~"streaming-*"}
- Thread dump location: /var/log/serving-runtime/thread-dumps/*.tdmp (collect latest from affected hosts)
- Quick rollback flags: --session.persist.mode=best-effort, --session.persist.compress=false

Notes to self:
- This one was subtle because Redis latency was not the biggest factor — the serialization path was. Good catch by on-call thread dumps. Runbook needs to be precise and the power to flip these flags must be quicker (one-click in console).

Owners and status tracker (short):
- Fix compression regression (Liam) — in progress.
- Runbook consolidation (Maya) — todo (draft in this doc).
- Circuit breaker design (Ravi) — design doc in progress.

End of document.
